title: Her – a poem inside a chronicle
short: 'Her' ('here', meaning 'in this year') is the standard first word of a Chronicle annal: the poem is the entry for 937 in the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle.
body: The poem has no title in the manuscripts. It is the annal for 937 in four manuscripts of the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle: A (the Parker Chronicle, Cambridge, Corpus Christi College 173), B, C and D (British Library, Cotton Tiberius A.vi, B.i and B.iv). A fifth copy, in Cotton Otho B.xi, was badly damaged in the 1731 fire and is known mainly from early transcripts. It opens with the annal formula 'Her', 'here [in this year]', so it is at once verse and record. It is one of several poems entered in the Chronicle in the tenth and eleventh centuries, praising the West Saxon royal house. Campbell's 1938 edition remains the standard commentary, and Livingston's Casebook (2011) collects the sources. Tennyson's verse translation (1880), made from his son Hallam's prose version, made the poem known to Victorian readers.

title: Æthelstan, king; 'lord of earls'
short: Æthelstan (king 924/5-939), grandson of Alfred, ruled all the English kingdoms; the poem gives him the heroic titles 'eorla dryhten' and 'beorna beahgifa'.
body: Æthelstan, son of Edward the Elder, became king of the West Saxons and Mercians in 924-925. In 927 he took York and became the first king to rule the whole of England. The 937 victory confirmed that position against a northern coalition. The poem gives him two traditional epithets in apposition: 'eorla dryhten' ('lord of noblemen') and 'beorna beahgifa' ('ring-giver of warriors'). 'Beahgifa' recalls the generous lord of heroic verse, who rewards his retinue with arm-rings ('beagas'). The style deliberately puts a contemporary West Saxon king into the language of Beowulf and Maldon. The alliteration in the first line falls on vowels: 'æþelstan' / 'eorla'.

title: Eadmund æþeling – Edmund the prince
short: Edmund, Æthelstan's younger half-brother, was then about sixteen. He succeeded him as king in 939 and ruled until 946.
body: 'Æþeling' means 'prince of the royal house', a man eligible for the throne. Edmund, born around 920-921, was a son of Edward the Elder by his third wife, Eadgifu. He fought alongside his half-brother and succeeded him in 939. The poem pairs the two throughout: 'he and his brother also' (l. 2), and at the end 'cyning and æþeling' going home together (l. 58). 'Ealdorlangne tir' (l. 3) means 'life-long glory', from 'ealdor', 'life' (not here 'chief'), and 'tir', 'glory'. 'Geslogon' means 'won by striking', from 'slean', so the glory is something earned in combat. 'Sweorda ecgum', 'with the edges of swords', is a common formula; a variant, 'sweordes ecgum', returns at l. 68.

title: Brunanburh – where was it?
short: The site of the battle is unknown and much argued over. Many scholars now favour Bromborough on the Wirral, but Lancashire, Yorkshire and Scottish sites have all had supporters.
body: 'Brunanburh' probably means 'Bruna's fortification' or 'the fort by the (river) Brune'. Other sources name the battle differently: 'Wendun' or 'Weondun' (Symeon of Durham), 'Brunandun', 'Vínheiðr' (Egils saga). The identification has been debated since the seventeenth century. The case for Bromborough on the Wirral, where the place-name can be derived from 'Brunanburh', has been put by Paul Cavill and others and is supported by Livingston's Casebook. It fits a Dublin fleet landing in the Mersey estuary (see 'Dinges mere', l. 54). Others have argued for sites in Lancashire, Yorkshire, the Scottish borders and elsewhere, and the question is still open. 'Ymbe' means 'around, near'.

title: The shield wall and 'leavings of hammers'
short: They split the shield wall and hacked the linden shields 'with the leavings of hammers', a kenning for swords forged by smiths.
body: 'Bordweal' ('board-wall') is the shield wall, the close formation of a Germanic battle line, also found in Maldon. 'Clufan' is the preterite plural of 'cleofan', 'to split'. 'Heaþolinde' means 'war-lindens', that is, shields, since they were made of lime-wood. 'Hamora lafan' is 'the leavings (remnants) of hammers', a kenning for swords: what the smith's hammer leaves behind. 'Laf' ('what is left, a remnant, heirloom') is a key word in the poem. The defeated go home as 'herelafum' ('remnants of the army', l. 47) and 'daraða laf' ('the spears' leavings', l. 54). This repeated use of 'laf' sets the victors' weapons against the vanquished survivors.

title: afaran Eadweardes – the sons of Edward
short: The victors are the 'offspring of Edward', the Elder (king 899-924). Their courage was 'natural to them from their ancestors', a praise of the West Saxon dynasty.
body: 'Afaran' (also 'eaforan') is a poetic word for 'offspring, sons'. Edward the Elder, son of Alfred, extended West Saxon rule over the Danelaw south of the Humber. 'Swa him geæþele wæs / from cneomægum' means 'as was natural to them from their kinsmen'. 'Geæþele', related to 'æþele', 'noble', here means 'inborn, natural', and 'cneomæg' is 'kinsman of a generation, ancestor'. The idea that courage is inherited through a royal line is central to the poem, which repeats the phrase 'Eadweardes afaran' at l. 52. 'Hord and hamas', 'treasure and homes' (l. 10), is an alliterating pair summing up what they defend. 'Ealgodon' is from 'ealgian', 'to defend'.

title: Scots and 'ship-sailors'
short: The enemy are the Scots under Constantine and the 'scipflotan', Norse seamen from Dublin under Anlaf. The Strathclyde Britons also fought, but the poem does not name them.
body: 'Sceotta leoda' means 'the people of the Scots'. 'Scipflotan' means 'ship-floaters', that is, seamen or vikings. Here they are the Hiberno-Norse of Dublin. Other sources show that the coalition included Owain of Strathclyde. 'Fæge' (l. 12) means 'fated to die, doomed', a word charged with heroic fatalism. 'Crungun' means 'fell (dead)', from 'cringan'. 'Feld dænnede / secga swate' says the field 'grew wet' (or 'resounded'; the verb is uncertain) with men's blood. The manuscripts spell the verb differently, and Campbell discusses its sense. 'Norþerna' (l. 18) and 'Scittisc' (l. 19) keep the two groups of enemies distinct.

title: The sun, 'God's bright candle'
short: The battle lasts from sunrise to sunset. The sun is 'the famous star' and 'God's bright candle', gliding over the land until it sinks to rest.
body: This is the poem's longest descriptive passage (ll. 13-17). 'Mære tungol' means 'glorious star'. 'Godes condel beorht, / eces drihtnes' is 'the bright candle of God, the eternal Lord', a kenning for the sun. 'Sio æþele gesceaft', 'the noble creation', is a further variation. 'Sah to setle' is 'sank to its seat', meaning set. 'Setl' is a seat, and the image is of the sun going to rest like a king to his throne or a man to his bed. The passage gives the battle a frame of a whole day ('ondlongne dæg', l. 21) and sets English victory within God's order. Beowulf calls the sun 'rodores candel' (l. 1572) and 'woruldcandel' (l. 1965), and 'candel' for a heavenly light is a common poetic usage.

title: eorodcistum – in troops; the pursuit
short: The West Saxons pursued 'in troops' all day long, cutting down fugitives from behind with swords 'sharp from the grindstone'.
body: 'Eorodcist' combines 'eored', 'troop, band (perhaps of horsemen)' (literally 'horse-riding', from 'eoh' + 'rad'), with 'cist', 'company'. It may mean mounted squadrons, which would suit a long pursuit, but editors are cautious. 'On last legdun' means 'laid on the track (of)', that is, followed close behind. 'Heowan herefleman hindan þearle' is 'they hewed the army-fugitives from behind fiercely'. 'Mylenscearp' (l. 24), 'mill-sharp', is a sword sharpened on a grindstone and is unique to this poem. Heroic poetry usually shames flight, so the stress on fugitives cut down from behind belittles the enemy.

title: Myrce ne wyrndon – litotes and 'hand-play'
short: 'The Mercians did not refuse hard hand-play to any of the warriors': an understatement meaning that they fought fiercely. Battle is described as 'play' all through the poem.
body: 'Myrce' are the Mercians. Naming them next to the West Saxons shows a joint English army, which fits Æthelstan's rule over both kingdoms. 'Ne wyrndon' ('did not refuse', from 'wyrnan') is litotes, typical of heroic style. 'Heardes hondplegan' means 'of hard hand-play'. 'Hondplega' is a kenning for combat, and 'plegan' returns ironically at l. 52 ('plegodan'), where the enemy 'played' with Edward's sons and lost. The poem has a run of such battle-kennings (ll. 49-51): 'cumbolgehnastes' ('clash of banners'), 'garmittinge' ('meeting of spears'), 'gumena gemotes' ('meeting of men'), 'wæpengewrixles' ('exchange of weapons'). Several of them are found only here.

title: æra gebland – the sea's tumult
short: 'Over the mingling of the waves', a poetic phrase for the sea that Anlaf's army crossed 'in the ship's bosom'.
body: 'Gebland' is 'mixture, commotion, tumult' (compare 'blandan', 'to mix'). The first word is usually explained from the poetic noun 'ear', 'sea, ocean'. So the phrase means 'the mingling of the waters', that is, the sea in motion. The manuscripts and editions spell it differently. 'On lides bosme' means 'in the ship's bosom', with 'lid' a poetic word for ship, used again at l. 34 ('to lides stefne', 'to the ship's prow'). The invaders came 'fæge to gefeohte', 'doomed to the fight'. The line therefore looks forward to their ruin, and the sea they crossed is the sea they will flee across. 'Gesohtun' means 'sought, came to'.

title: Five young kings and seven earls
short: The poem counts the dead: five young kings and seven of Anlaf's earls, 'put to sleep by swords', and a countless host besides.
body: 'Lægun' is 'lay (dead)'. 'Cyningas giunge', 'young kings', are probably lesser Norse or Gaelic kings and sub-kings of the coalition. The poem names none of them, and other sources' lists cannot be reconciled with certainty. 'Sweordum aswefede' means 'put to sleep by swords', a euphemism for killing, from 'aswebban', 'to lull to sleep, kill'. The counting ('fife ... seofene ... unrim', 'countless') reads like an annal, but the euphemism is poetic. 'Campstede' means 'battlefield' ('camp', 'battle', from Latin 'campus'). 'Unrim heriges' means 'a countless number of the army'.

title: Anlaf, 'chief of the Northmen', and his escape
short: Anlaf (Óláfr Guthfrithson, king of Dublin, d. 941) is driven to his ship 'with a small company' and escapes onto the dark flood, saving his life.
body: 'Anlaf' is the English form of Old Norse 'Óláfr'. He was Óláfr Guthfrithson, king of Dublin, who claimed York. 'Bregu' (also 'brego') is a poetic word for 'prince, chief'. 'Nede gebeded' means 'compelled by necessity'. 'Litle weorode', 'with a little troop', echoes the heroic shame of a lord without followers. 'Cread cnear on flot' means 'the ship pressed out onto the water'. 'Cread' is from 'crudan', 'to press, hasten'. 'Cnear' (compare 'negledcnearrum', 'nail-studded ships', l. 53) is a loan from Old Norse 'knǫrr', a merchant or sea-going ship. 'Feorh generede', 'saved his life', is ironic: the leader survives as his men die. 'Fealene flod' means 'the fallow/dark flood'.

title: Constantine, the 'old grey warrior'
short: Constantine II, king of the Scots (r. c. 900-943), flees north. He lost kinsmen and friends, and left his young son dead on the field.
body: Constantine son of Áed ruled Alba from about 900 until he became a monk at St Andrews in the 940s. He had submitted to Æthelstan in 927 and was invaded by him in 934, and he was the senior member of the 937 coalition. 'Se froda' ('the old, experienced one') and 'har hilderinc' ('grey-haired battle-man') stress his age. The poem then uses irony: 'hreman ne þorfte / mæca gemanan', he had no cause to exult in the fellowship of swords. 'He wæs his mæga sceard' means 'he was deprived of his kinsmen', with 'sceard', 'cut off from, bereft'. His son is 'wundun forgrunden', 'ground to pieces by wounds'.

title: No cause to boast: the poem's taunting
short: 'The grey-haired man had no need to boast of the sword-clash ... nor Anlaf any more'. The poem mocks the losers with repeated 'ne þorfte'.
body: 'Gelpan' (West Saxon 'gielpan') means 'to boast', and 'gylp' is a warrior's vow or boast in heroic verse. 'Ne þorfte' ('had no need') is used three times (ll. 39, 44, 47), each time about the enemy. It is ironic understatement: they had nothing to boast or laugh about. 'Beorn blandenfeax', 'grey-haired warrior', uses 'blanden-', 'mixed', for hair streaked with grey. 'Bilgeslehtes' means 'clash of swords' ('bill' + 'geslieht'). 'Eald inwidda' means 'old malicious enemy'. 'Hlehhan' ('to laugh', l. 47) refers to the enemy's hopes of victory. The phrase 'þæt heo beaduweorca beteran wurdun' ('that they were the better in battle-work') sums up the boast they cannot make. Critics often read the tone as close to the triumphal mockery of a victory song.

title: Dinges mere – a crux of place
short: The Norse ships leave 'on Dinges mere' for Dublin. The phrase is obscure, and recent work links it with the Thingwall area of the Wirral.
body: 'On Dinges mere' has been read in several ways. Some take it as the open sea ('mere', 'sea, lake'), with 'Dinges' as an obscure name or a corruption. Others see a place-name. Paul Cavill and others have connected it with the Norse assembly site ('þing') at Thingwall on the Wirral and a nearby stretch of water. That would support the identification of Brunanburh with Bromborough. Others remain unconvinced. 'Dreorig daraða laf' means 'the bloody remnant of spears', those whom the spears left alive. 'Darað' is 'spear, dart'. 'Æwiscmode' (l. 56) means 'ashamed, disgraced in mind'. 'Difelin' is Dublin, and 'Iraland' Ireland.

title: daraða laf – what the spears left
short: 'The bloody remnant of spears' turns the kenning 'leavings of hammers' back on the defeated: they are what the weapons left behind.
body: 'Darað' is a rare poetic word for 'spear, javelin'. It may be connected with Old Norse 'darraðr', though the relation is uncertain. 'Laf' (remnant, leavings) has already appeared in 'hamora lafan', 'leavings of hammers' (l. 6), meaning swords, and in 'herelafum', 'army-remnants' (l. 47). Here the defeated Norse are described as what is left over after the spears have done their work. Repeating the same word gives the poem an ironic symmetry. The English strike with what hammers made, and the enemy go home as what spears left. 'Negledcnearrum' (l. 53) means 'in nail-fastened ships', clinker-built vessels.

title: The beasts of battle
short: The raven, the eagle and the wolf are left to share the corpses. This is the traditional 'beasts of battle' theme of Old English heroic verse.
body: 'Hræw bryttian' means 'to divide/enjoy the corpses' ('bryttian', 'to distribute, share out', as a lord shares treasure). The beasts are the black raven, dark-coated ('saluwigpada') and horny-beaked ('hyrnednebba'). Then there is the grey-coated ('hasewanpada') eagle, 'white behind' ('æftan hwit'), which is probably the white-tailed sea eagle, a 'greedy war-hawk' ('guðhafoc'). Last is 'the grey beast, the wolf in the forest'. 'Æses brucan', 'to enjoy the carrion', completes the grim feast. Magoun (1955) identified this trio as a recurring theme in Old English heroic poetry, found in Judith, Exodus, Maldon and elsewhere, and usually placed before or after battle. Here it marks the end of the battle. The descriptive compounds, several rare, are among the most elaborate examples of the theme.

title: 'As books tell us': the coming of the English
short: The poem ends by claiming that no greater slaughter had happened on the island since the Angles and Saxons came from the east, 'as books tell us, old scholars'.
body: 'Bec' are books, and 'ealde uðwitan' are 'old wise men, scholars, philosophers' ('uðwita' translates Latin 'philosophus'). The poet appeals to written history, not oral memory, and this suits a poem in a chronicle. The reference is to the 'Adventus Saxonum' as told by Bede (Historia ecclesiastica I.15) and the Chronicle annals for 449. The Angles and Saxons came 'eastan', from the east, over 'brad brimu', the broad seas, overcame the Britons ('Wealas'), and won the land ('eard begeatan'). They are 'wlance wigsmiþas' ('proud war-smiths') and 'eorlas arhwate' ('nobles eager for glory'). The ending sets Æthelstan's victory in a long history of conquest. Critics have noted the irony that the English, now defending their land against invaders, are celebrated as invaders themselves.
